blocks.en: "Immediately I was in the Spirit; and behold, a throne set in heaven, and One sat on the throne... 'You are worthy... for You were slain, and have redeemed us to God by Your blood.'" — Revelation 4:2; 5:9 (NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: "Al instante yo estaba en el Espíritu; y he aquí, un trono que estaba puesto en el cielo, y sobre el trono uno sentado... 'Digno eres... porque tú fuiste inmolado, y nos has redimido para Dios con tu sangre.'" — Apocalipsis 4:2; 5:9 (RVG)

blocks.en: A Door Standing Open in Heaven
blocks.es_reference: Una Puerta Abierta en el Cielo

blocks.en: With the letters to the seven churches finished, the scene changes. "After these things I looked, and behold, a door standing open in heaven. And the first voice which I heard was like a trumpet speaking with me, saying, 'Come up here, and I will show you things which must take place after this'" (Revelation 4:1). The reader is lifted from earth, where the churches struggle, into heaven itself, the realm of unseen reality that lies behind and above everything we can see. As in chapter one, John says, "Immediately I was in the Spirit" (Revelation 4:2), the phrase that marks the great visions of the book; he is carried by the Holy Spirit into a sight no natural eye could reach. The summons "Come up here" has been read in more than one way: some hear in it a foreshadowing of the church's being caught up to be with Christ, while others take it simply as John's own call to ascend in vision, and the course leaves the question open. What is certain is that the curtain is drawn back, and the rest of the book will be understood only from this vantage point, looking at the troubles of earth from the throne room of heaven.
blocks.es_reference: Terminadas las cartas a las siete iglesias, la escena cambia. "Después de estas cosas miré, y he aquí una puerta abierta en el cielo; y la primera voz que oí, era como de trompeta que hablaba conmigo, diciendo: Sube acá, y yo te mostraré las cosas que han de ser después de éstas" (Apocalipsis 4:1). El lector es levantado de la tierra, donde las iglesias luchan, hasta el cielo mismo, el reino de la realidad invisible que está detrás y por encima de todo lo que podemos ver. Como en el capítulo uno, Juan dice: "Al instante yo estaba en el Espíritu" (Apocalipsis 4:2), la frase que marca las grandes visiones del libro; es llevado por el Espíritu Santo a una vista que ningún ojo natural podría alcanzar. El llamado "Sube acá" se ha entendido de más de una manera: algunos oyen en él una prefiguración de que la iglesia sea arrebatada para estar con Cristo, mientras que otros lo toman simplemente como el llamado de Juan a ascender en visión, y el curso deja la pregunta abierta. Lo cierto es que se descorre la cortina, y el resto del libro se entenderá solo desde este punto de vista, mirando los problemas de la tierra desde la sala del trono del cielo.

blocks.en: One Seated on the Throne
blocks.es_reference: Uno Sentado sobre el Trono

blocks.en: The first thing John sees, and the center of everything that follows, is a throne. "Behold, a throne set in heaven, and One sat on the throne" (Revelation 4:2). The throne is the focal point of the entire book of Revelation; before any seal is opened, any trumpet sounded, or any bowl poured out, the reader is shown that God is seated, sovereign, and in command of all. John does not attempt to describe the One on the throne by face or form, but only by the flash of precious stones: He was "like a jasper and a sardius stone in appearance; and there was a rainbow around the throne, in appearance like an emerald" (Revelation 4:3). The brilliance speaks of a holiness and majesty too great for words, and the encircling rainbow recalls God's covenant mercy, the promise that His judgments are always ringed about with grace. Whatever storms break upon the earth in the chapters to come, this is the unchanging fact behind them all: a throne stands in heaven, and God is on it.
blocks.es_reference: Lo primero que Juan ve, y el centro de todo lo que sigue, es un trono. "He aquí, un trono que estaba puesto en el cielo, y sobre el trono uno sentado" (Apocalipsis 4:2). El trono es el punto focal de todo el libro del Apocalipsis; antes de que se abra un sello, suene una trompeta, o se derrame una copa, se le muestra al lector que Dios está sentado, soberano, y al mando de todo. Juan no intenta describir al que está sobre el trono por rostro o forma, sino solo por el destello de piedras preciosas: era "semejante a una piedra de jaspe y de sardio; y había alrededor del trono un arco iris, semejante en aspecto a la esmeralda" (Apocalipsis 4:3). El resplandor habla de una santidad y majestad demasiado grandes para palabras, y el arco iris que lo rodea recuerda la misericordia del pacto de Dios, la promesa de que sus juicios siempre están rodeados de gracia. Cualesquiera tormentas estallen sobre la tierra en los capítulos por venir, este es el hecho inmutable detrás de todas ellas: un trono está puesto en el cielo, y Dios está sobre él.

blocks.en: The Elders and the Living Creatures
blocks.es_reference: Los Ancianos y los Cuatro Animales

blocks.en: Around the throne John sees two circles of worshipers. First, "around the throne were twenty-four thrones, and on the thrones I saw twenty-four elders sitting, clothed in white robes; and they had crowns of gold on their heads" (Revelation 4:4). Their white robes speak of purity and their golden crowns of reward and reign. Who they are has been understood in more than one way: many take them as the redeemed people of God, perhaps the union of Israel and the church in their twelve-and-twelve numbers; others see an exalted order of heavenly beings; the course presents the views fairly and does not insist on one. From the throne proceed "lightnings, thunderings, and voices," and before it burn "seven lamps of fire, which are the seven Spirits of God" (Revelation 4:5), a picture of the fullness of the Holy Spirit. Before the throne stretches what looks like "a sea of glass, like crystal" (Revelation 4:6), a floor of stillness and clarity. And in the midst are four living creatures full of eyes, one like a lion, one like a calf, one with a face like a man, and one like a flying eagle — beings much like the cherubim of Ezekiel and the seraphim of Isaiah, covered with eyes to show that nothing escapes their sight as they guard the throne of God.
blocks.es_reference: Alrededor del trono Juan ve dos círculos de adoradores. Primero, "alrededor del trono había veinticuatro tronos; y vi sobre los tronos veinticuatro ancianos sentados, vestidos de ropas blancas; y tenían sobre sus cabezas coronas de oro" (Apocalipsis 4:4). Sus ropas blancas hablan de pureza y sus coronas de oro de galardón y reinado. Quiénes son se ha entendido de más de una manera: muchos los toman como el pueblo redimido de Dios, quizás la unión de Israel y la iglesia en sus números de doce y doce; otros ven un orden exaltado de seres celestiales; el curso presenta las visiones con justicia y no insiste en una. Del trono salen "relámpagos y truenos y voces," y delante de él arden "siete lámparas de fuego, las cuales son los siete Espíritus de Dios" (Apocalipsis 4:5), una imagen de la plenitud del Espíritu Santo. Delante del trono se extiende lo que parece "un mar de vidrio semejante al cristal" (Apocalipsis 4:6), un piso de quietud y claridad. Y en medio están cuatro animales llenos de ojos, uno semejante a un león, otro a un becerro, otro con rostro como de hombre, y otro como un águila volando — seres muy parecidos a los querubines de Ezequiel y los serafines de Isaías, cubiertos de ojos para mostrar que nada escapa a su vista mientras guardan el trono de Dios.

blocks.en: Holy, Holy, Holy: The Worship of the Creator
blocks.es_reference: Santo, Santo, Santo: La Adoración del Creador

blocks.en: The living creatures never cease their cry, "Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Almighty, who was and is and is to come!" (Revelation 4:8). The threefold "holy" lifts up the perfect, unapproachable purity of God, and the title "who was and is and is to come" declares Him the eternal Lord of all time. As often as the creatures give glory, the twenty-four elders fall down before the throne and do a striking thing: they cast their crowns before it, surrendering every honor they have been given back to the One who gave it (Revelation 4:10). Their song names the ground of this first great act of worship: "You are worthy, O Lord, to receive glory and honor and power; for You created all things, and by Your will they exist and were created" (Revelation 4:11). Here God is worshiped as Creator. Because He made all things and holds them in being by His will, He alone is worthy of glory, and every crown in heaven belongs at His feet. Chapter four sets the throne and the worship of the Creator before us, and only then does the book move to the question that will fill chapter five.
blocks.es_reference: Los animales no cesan su clamor: "Santo, santo, santo, Señor Dios Todopoderoso, el que era, el que es, y el que ha de venir" (Apocalipsis 4:8). El triple "santo" exalta la pureza perfecta e inaccesible de Dios, y el título "el que era, el que es, y el que ha de venir" lo declara el Señor eterno de todo tiempo. Cada vez que los animales dan gloria, los veinticuatro ancianos se postran delante del trono y hacen algo impactante: echan sus coronas delante de él, entregando todo honor que se les ha dado de vuelta al que se lo dio (Apocalipsis 4:10). Su cántico nombra el fundamento de este primer gran acto de adoración: "Señor, digno eres de recibir gloria y honra y poder; porque tú creaste todas las cosas, y por tu voluntad existen y fueron creadas" (Apocalipsis 4:11). Aquí Dios es adorado como Creador. Porque hizo todas las cosas y las sostiene en existencia por su voluntad, solo él es digno de gloria, y toda corona en el cielo pertenece a sus pies. El capítulo cuatro pone delante de nosotros el trono y la adoración del Creador, y solo entonces el libro pasa a la pregunta que llenará el capítulo cinco.

blocks.en: The Sealed Scroll and the Lion Who Is a Lamb
blocks.es_reference: El Libro Sellado y el León que Es un Cordero

blocks.en: "And I saw in the right hand of Him who sat on the throne a scroll written inside and on the back, sealed with seven seals" (Revelation 5:1). The sealed scroll is best understood as the unfolding plan and purpose of God for all history, the title-deed to the world, which cannot take effect until someone is found worthy to break its seals. A strong angel cries out, "Who is worthy to open the scroll and to loose its seals?" (Revelation 5:2), and the silence is total: no one in heaven, on earth, or under the earth could open it. John weeps much at this, for if no one can open the scroll, then God's purposes seem to stall and history has no redeemer. Then one of the elders comforts him: "Do not weep. Behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has prevailed to open the scroll" (Revelation 5:5). John turns to see the conquering Lion — and sees instead "a Lamb as though it had been slain" (Revelation 5:6). This is the heart of the vision. The mighty Lion of Judah, the King of all, has triumphed, but He triumphed by being slain; He still bears the marks of the One whose throat was cut as a sacrifice. The Lion and the Lamb are the same Person, and He conquers not by force but by His own death. The Lamb has seven horns and seven eyes, the fullness of power and of the Spirit sent into all the earth, and He steps forward and takes the scroll from the right hand of Him who sits on the throne.
blocks.es_reference: "Y vi en la mano derecha del que estaba sentado sobre el trono un libro escrito por dentro y por fuera, sellado con siete sellos" (Apocalipsis 5:1). El libro sellado se entiende mejor como el plan y propósito desplegado de Dios para toda la historia, el título de propiedad del mundo, que no puede tener efecto hasta que se halle a alguien digno de romper sus sellos. Un ángel fuerte clama: "¿Quién es digno de abrir el libro y desatar sus sellos?" (Apocalipsis 5:2), y el silencio es total: ninguno en el cielo, ni en la tierra, ni debajo de la tierra podía abrirlo. Juan llora mucho ante esto, pues si ninguno puede abrir el libro, entonces los propósitos de Dios parecen detenerse y la historia no tiene redentor. Entonces uno de los ancianos lo consuela: "No llores; he aquí que el León de la tribu de Judá, la raíz de David, ha vencido para abrir el libro" (Apocalipsis 5:5). Juan se vuelve para ver al León vencedor — y ve en cambio "un Cordero como inmolado" (Apocalipsis 5:6). Este es el corazón de la visión. El poderoso León de Judá, el Rey de todo, ha triunfado, pero triunfó siendo inmolado; aún lleva las marcas de aquel cuya garganta fue cortada como sacrificio. El León y el Cordero son la misma Persona, y vence no por la fuerza sino por su propia muerte. El Cordero tiene siete cuernos y siete ojos, la plenitud del poder y del Espíritu enviado a toda la tierra, y se adelanta y toma el libro de la mano derecha del que está sentado sobre el trono.

blocks.en: The New Song: Worthy Is the Lamb
blocks.es_reference: El Nuevo Cántico: Digno Es el Cordero

blocks.en: The moment the Lamb takes the scroll, heaven erupts in worship. The four living creatures and the twenty-four elders fall down before Him, each holding a harp and "golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints" (Revelation 5:8) — a tender detail, that the prayers of struggling believers on earth are gathered up and treasured in heaven. They sing a new song: "You are worthy to take the scroll, and to open its seals; for You were slain, and have redeemed us to God by Your blood out of every tribe and tongue and people and nation, and have made us kings and priests to our God" (Revelation 5:9-10). The Lamb is worthy because He was slain and by His blood purchased a people for God from every nation on earth, making them a kingdom of priests. Then the circle of worship widens. John hears the voice of countless angels around the throne, ten thousand times ten thousand and thousands of thousands, all saying with a loud voice, "Worthy is the Lamb who was slain to receive power and riches and wisdom and strength and honor and glory and blessing!" (Revelation 5:12). What chapter four gave to the Creator, chapter five now gives to the Lamb.
blocks.es_reference: En el momento en que el Cordero toma el libro, el cielo estalla en adoración. Los cuatro animales y los veinticuatro ancianos se postran delante de él, cada uno con un arpa y "copas de oro llenas de incienso, que son las oraciones de los santos" (Apocalipsis 5:8) — un detalle tierno, que las oraciones de los creyentes que luchan en la tierra son recogidas y atesoradas en el cielo. Cantan un nuevo cántico: "Digno eres de tomar el libro y de abrir sus sellos; porque tú fuiste inmolado, y nos has redimido para Dios con tu sangre, de todo linaje y lengua y pueblo y nación; y nos has hecho para nuestro Dios reyes y sacerdotes" (Apocalipsis 5:9-10). El Cordero es digno porque fue inmolado y por su sangre compró un pueblo para Dios de toda nación de la tierra, haciéndolos un reino de sacerdotes. Luego el círculo de adoración se ensancha. Juan oye la voz de innumerables ángeles alrededor del trono, millones de millones, todos diciendo a gran voz: "El Cordero que fue inmolado es digno de tomar el poder y riquezas y sabiduría y fortaleza y honra y gloria y alabanza" (Apocalipsis 5:12). Lo que el capítulo cuatro dio al Creador, el capítulo cinco ahora lo da al Cordero.

blocks.en: Every Creature Worships the Lamb
blocks.es_reference: Toda Criatura Adora al Cordero

blocks.en: The worship spreads until it fills the whole creation. "And every creature which is in heaven and on the earth and under the earth and such as are in the sea, and all that are in them, I heard saying: 'Blessing and honor and glory and power be to Him who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb, forever and ever!'" (Revelation 5:13). This final doxology is addressed to two and yet sounds as one: to Him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb together. The slain Lamb receives the very worship given to God on the throne, which is among the clearest declarations in all of Scripture that Jesus Christ is fully God and shares the throne of heaven. The four living creatures answer "Amen!" and the elders fall down and worship (Revelation 5:14). So the two chapters set the stage for everything that follows. Whatever seals are about to be opened, whatever judgments are about to fall, history is utterly safe, because the One on the throne reigns over all and the slain Lamb has prevailed and holds the scroll. The right response, in heaven and on earth, is worship.
blocks.es_reference: La adoración se extiende hasta llenar toda la creación. "Y oí a toda criatura que está en el cielo, y sobre la tierra, y debajo de la tierra, y que está en el mar, y todas las cosas que en ellos hay, diciendo: Al que está sentado en el trono, y al Cordero, sea la alabanza, y la honra, y la gloria, y el poder, para siempre jamás" (Apocalipsis 5:13). Esta doxología final se dirige a dos y sin embargo suena como una: al que está sentado en el trono y al Cordero juntos. El Cordero inmolado recibe la misma adoración dada a Dios en el trono, lo cual es una de las declaraciones más claras de toda la Escritura de que Jesucristo es plenamente Dios y comparte el trono del cielo. Los cuatro animales responden "Amén," y los ancianos se postran y adoran (Apocalipsis 5:14). Así los dos capítulos preparan el escenario para todo lo que sigue. Cualesquiera sellos estén por abrirse, cualesquiera juicios estén por caer, la historia está completamente segura, porque el que está sobre el trono reina sobre todo y el Cordero inmolado ha vencido y tiene el libro. La respuesta correcta, en el cielo y en la tierra, es la adoración.

blocks.en: "Worthy is the Lamb who was slain to receive power and riches and wisdom and strength and honor and glory and blessing!" — Revelation 5:12 (NKJV)

mc.stem: As chapters 4-5 open, the scene of the vision shifts from the churches on earth to:
options: Heaven, the throne room of God
mc.why: A door opens in heaven and John is taken up into the throne room (4:1-2).

mc.stem: As the heavenly vision begins, John is "in the Spirit" and the first thing he sees is:
options: A throne set in heaven, with One seated on it
mc.why: "A throne set in heaven, and One sat on the throne" (4:2).

mc.stem: The dominant feature of the heavenly vision, the focal point of the whole book, is:
mc.why: The throne is central; God is shown seated and sovereign before anything else (4:2).

mc.stem: Around the throne John saw twenty-four elders in white robes wearing:
mc.why: They had crowns of gold on their heads (4:4).

mc.stem: The seven lamps of fire burning before the throne are identified as:
mc.why: The seven lamps are the seven Spirits of God (4:5).

mc.stem: The four living creatures full of eyes resemble the heavenly beings in the visions of:
mc.why: They are like the cherubim of Ezekiel and the seraphim of Isaiah (4:6-8).

mc.stem: The ceaseless cry of the four living creatures around the throne is:
options: Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Almighty
mc.why: "Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Almighty" (4:8).

mc.stem: In chapter 4 God is worshiped especially in His character as:
mc.why: "You created all things" — God worshiped as Creator (4:11).

mc.stem: The twenty-four elders express their worship by:
options: Casting their crowns before the throne
mc.why: They cast their crowns before the throne (4:10).

mc.stem: The scroll in the right hand of the One on the throne was sealed with:
mc.why: The scroll was sealed with seven seals (5:1).

mc.stem: John wept much in chapter 5 because:
options: No one was found worthy to open the scroll
mc.why: No one in heaven or earth was found worthy to open the scroll (5:3-4).

mc.stem: One of the elders comforted John by announcing the triumph of:
options: The Lion of the tribe of Judah
mc.why: "The Lion of the tribe of Judah... has prevailed" (5:5).

mc.stem: When John looked to see the conquering Lion, he saw instead:
options: A Lamb as though it had been slain
mc.why: The Lion is revealed as a Lamb that had been slain (5:6).

mc.stem: The Lamb's seven horns and seven eyes signify:
options: His complete power and the seven Spirits sent into all the earth
mc.why: Seven horns and eyes: full power and the seven Spirits sent into all the earth (5:6).

mc.stem: The golden bowls of incense held by the elders are explained as:
mc.why: The bowls of incense are the prayers of the saints (5:8).

mc.stem: The "new song" praises the Lamb because by His blood He has:
options: Redeemed people from every tribe, tongue, and nation
mc.why: He redeemed people to God by His blood from every tribe and nation (5:9).

mc.stem: By His blood the Lamb has made the redeemed to be:
mc.why: He made them kings and priests to our God (5:10).

mc.stem: The number of angels surrounding the throne is described as:
mc.why: Ten thousand times ten thousand and thousands of thousands (5:11).

mc.stem: At the climax, the same worship is given both to Him on the throne and to the Lamb, which points to:
options: The full deity of Christ, who shares God's throne
mc.why: Worship of the Lamb alongside God declares Christ's full deity (5:13).

mc.stem: The central truth of chapters 4-5, underlying all the judgments to come, is that:
options: The church will escape all trouble
God reigns on the throne and the slain Lamb has prevailed to open the scroll
mc.why: God reigns and the worthy Lamb holds history's scroll; history is safe (4-5).

sa.prompt: Describe the opening of the heavenly vision in Revelation 4:1-2: the open door, the call "come up here," and being "in the Spirit."
sa.model: After the letters to the seven churches, the scene changes. John sees a door standing open in heaven, and a voice like a trumpet calls, Come up here, and I will show you what must take place. He is lifted from the earth, where the churches struggle, into heaven itself, the realm of unseen reality behind all that we can see. As in chapter one, he says he was immediately in the Spirit, the phrase that marks the great visions of the book, for he is carried by the Holy Spirit into a sight no natural eye could reach. The call come up here has been understood in more than one way, some hearing a foreshadowing of the church being caught up to Christ and others taking it simply as John's own summons to ascend in vision, and the course leaves the question open. What is certain is that the curtain is drawn back, and the rest of the book is to be read from this vantage point, looking at the troubles of earth from the throne room of heaven.

sa.prompt: Describe the throne and the One seated on it, and explain why the throne is so central to Revelation.
sa.model: The first thing John sees, and the center of everything that follows, is a throne set in heaven with One seated on it. The throne is the focal point of the whole book of Revelation, for before any seal is opened, any trumpet sounded, or any bowl poured out, the reader is shown that God is seated, sovereign, and in command of all. John does not describe the One on the throne by face or form but only by the flash of precious stones, like jasper and sardius, with a rainbow like an emerald around the throne. The brilliance speaks of a holiness and majesty too great for words, and the encircling rainbow recalls God's covenant mercy, so that His judgments are always ringed about with grace. This is why the throne is central: whatever storms break upon the earth in the chapters to come, the unchanging fact behind them all is that a throne stands in heaven and God reigns upon it. The vision steadies the believer by fixing his eyes first on the sovereign God before any trouble is shown.

sa.prompt: Who are the twenty-four elders and the four living creatures around the throne?
sa.model: Around the throne John sees two circles of worshipers. First are twenty-four elders seated on thrones, clothed in white robes, with crowns of gold on their heads, the white speaking of purity and the crowns of reward and reign. Who they are has been understood in more than one way: many take them as the redeemed people of God, perhaps Israel and the church together in their twelve-and-twelve numbers, while others see an exalted order of heavenly beings, and the course presents the views fairly without insisting on one. Second are four living creatures full of eyes, one like a lion, one like a calf, one with a face like a man, and one like a flying eagle. They are much like the cherubim of Ezekiel and the seraphim of Isaiah, and their many eyes show that nothing escapes their sight as they guard the throne and lead the worship of God. Together with the seven lamps that are the seven Spirits of God and the sea of glass, they fill the throne room with reverence.

sa.prompt: Explain the worship of God as Creator in Revelation 4 ("Holy, holy, holy" and the casting of crowns).
sa.model: The four living creatures never cease to cry, Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Almighty, who was and is and is to come. The threefold holy lifts up the perfect, unapproachable purity of God, and the title who was and is and is to come declares Him the eternal Lord of all time. As often as the creatures give glory, the twenty-four elders fall down and cast their crowns before the throne, surrendering every honor they have been given back to the One who gave it. Their song names the ground of this worship: You are worthy, O Lord, to receive glory and honor and power, for You created all things, and by Your will they exist and were created. Here God is worshiped specifically as Creator. Because He made all things and holds them in being by His will, He alone is worthy of glory, and every crown in heaven belongs at His feet. Chapter four fixes the worship of the Creator in view before the book turns to the sealed scroll and the Lamb.

sa.prompt: What is the sealed scroll, and why could no one open it, and why did John weep?
sa.model: In the right hand of the One on the throne John sees a scroll written inside and on the back and sealed with seven seals. The scroll is best understood as the unfolding plan and purpose of God for all history, the title-deed to the world, which cannot take effect until someone worthy is found to break its seals. A strong angel cries, Who is worthy to open the scroll and loose its seals, and the silence is total, for no one in heaven, on earth, or under the earth was able to open it or even to look at it. John weeps much at this, because if no one can open the scroll, then God's purposes seem to stall and history has no redeemer to carry them through. His tears show how much hangs on the question of who is worthy. The weeping does not last, for an elder will point him to the One who has prevailed, but it underscores that the whole plan of God for the world waits on a worthy hand to open the scroll.

sa.prompt: Explain how the Lion of Judah turns out to be a slain Lamb, and what this reveals about the way Christ conquers.
sa.model: When John weeps, an elder comforts him: do not weep, for the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has prevailed to open the scroll. John turns to see the conquering Lion, and instead he sees a Lamb as though it had been slain. This is the heart of the vision. The mighty Lion of Judah, the King of all, has truly triumphed, but He triumphed by being slain, and He still bears the marks of one offered up as a sacrifice. The Lion and the Lamb are the same Person, and the point is that He conquers not by force or violence but by His own death and shed blood. The victory that opens history's scroll was won at the cross. This reframes what power and triumph mean: the strongest act in the universe was the Lamb laying down His life. So the One worthy to take the scroll is worthy precisely because He was slain, and the redeemed will praise Him forever as the Lamb who conquered by being slain for them.

sa.prompt: Describe the Lamb that John sees (His seven horns and seven eyes) and what He does with the scroll.
sa.model: The figure John sees in the midst of the throne is a Lamb as though it had been slain, bearing the marks of sacrifice yet alive and standing. The Lamb has seven horns and seven eyes. In Scripture the horn is a symbol of power, so seven horns picture His complete and perfect power, and the seven eyes are explained as the seven Spirits of God sent out into all the earth, picturing His full possession of the Spirit and His all-seeing presence everywhere. Then the Lamb does what no one else in all creation could do: He steps forward and takes the scroll out of the right hand of Him who sits on the throne. This single act answers John's tears and changes everything, for the One worthy to open the scroll has come and has taken it into His hand. The plan of God for history is now safe in the hand of the slain and risen Lamb, who has the power and the Spirit to carry it through to the end.

sa.prompt: Explain the "new song" of Revelation 5 and what it declares the Lamb accomplished by His blood.
sa.model: The moment the Lamb takes the scroll, the living creatures and the elders fall down before Him, each with a harp and golden bowls of incense, which are explained as the prayers of the saints, a tender sign that the prayers of struggling believers are treasured in heaven. They sing a new song: You are worthy to take the scroll and to open its seals, for You were slain, and have redeemed us to God by Your blood out of every tribe and tongue and people and nation, and have made us kings and priests to our God. The song declares why the Lamb is worthy: He was slain, and by His shed blood He purchased a people for God out of every nation on earth, gathering a worldwide family and making them a kingdom of priests who will reign. The new song is the song of redemption, and it could not have been sung before the cross. It centers all the worship of heaven on what the Lamb has done in saving sinners by His blood.

sa.prompt: Describe the widening circles of worship in Revelation 5 and what the worship of the Lamb reveals about who He is.
sa.model: The worship in chapter five widens in ever larger circles. First the living creatures and elders sing the new song to the Lamb. Then John hears countless angels around the throne, thousands of thousands, crying with a loud voice, Worthy is the Lamb who was slain to receive power and riches and wisdom and strength and honor and glory and blessing. Finally the circle takes in the whole creation, every creature in heaven and on earth and under the earth and in the sea, saying, Blessing and honor and glory and power be to Him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb forever and ever. This final praise is given to two and yet sounds as one, to God on the throne and to the Lamb together. The fact that the slain Lamb receives the very worship given to God is among the clearest declarations in Scripture that Jesus Christ is fully God and shares the throne of heaven. The living creatures answer Amen, and the elders fall down and worship, sealing the truth that the Lamb is worthy of all the glory due to God.

sa.prompt: Summarize the central truth of Unit 5: what do the throne of chapter 4 and the Lamb of chapter 5 establish for the rest of the book?
sa.model: The central truth of Unit 5 is set by two chapters that belong together. Chapter four shows the throne in heaven with God seated upon it, sovereign over all, worshiped without ceasing as the holy Creator, with every crown cast at His feet. Chapter five shows the sealed scroll of history, which no one was worthy to open, and then the Lion of Judah who is a slain Lamb, the only One worthy to take the scroll and open its seals, worshiped by the whole creation as the Redeemer who bought a people by His blood. Together they establish the foundation for everything that follows. Before any seal is broken or any judgment falls in the chapters to come, the reader knows that God reigns on the throne and that the slain and risen Lamb has prevailed and holds the scroll of history in His hand. Therefore history is utterly safe, guided by a sovereign God and a worthy Lamb, and the right response, in heaven and on earth, is worship.
